# Future Directions — No-Stretching of Quotient Labelings from Edge Partitions

These conjectures grew out of a single structural discovery: when the edges of a
connected graph are partitioned into classes and each class is assigned a generator
of an elementary abelian 2-group, the resulting vertex labeling never *stretches*
distances into the Cayley graph on those generators, but it can and does fail to be
Hamming-nonexpanding once cycles force a generator to become a combination of others.
The correct ambient object is therefore the Cayley graph on the class generators, not
the coordinate hypercube.

## 1. Corank governs the isometry defect

**Conjecture.** For a connected graph with an edge partition into `t` classes whose
cycle-class parity space has rank `r`, the maximum stretch of the quotient labeling
when read into the coordinate hypercube on `t − r` coordinates is bounded by, and
generically equal to, a monotone function of `r`; in particular the labeling is
isometric into some coordinate hypercube if and only if `r = 0` on every induced
even-cycle subspace.

**The key insight is** that the only obstruction to a genuine hypercube embedding is a
cycle whose class-parity vector is nonzero, and each independent such cycle contributes
exactly one "folded" coordinate that a coordinate reading double-counts.

**Why now?** Distance-labeling schemes for routing and for graph-similarity search are
increasingly built from cheap parity sketches; knowing precisely when a parity sketch is
lossless (isometric) versus merely one-sided (no-stretch) tells a system designer when a
sketch can certify a lower bound on true distance for free.

## 2. One-sided labelings certify lower bounds at scale

**Conjecture.** Any labeling that maps adjacent vertices to adjacent-or-equal vertices of
a fixed target graph yields a distance oracle that is never an over-estimate of the target
distance and never an under-estimate of the source distance simultaneously; consequently a
family of such labelings into small Cayley graphs can certify multiplicative
lower bounds on graph distance using space independent of the number of vertices.

**The key insight is** that non-expansion is preserved under taking maxima over a family of
edge-contracting maps, so many weak one-sided sketches combine into one strong certificate.

**Why now?** Sublinear-space distance certification is a live demand in graph databases;
one-sided guarantees are exactly what verifiable query engines need, because a certified
lower bound cannot be gamed by an adversarial index.

## 3. Median graphs are the fixed point of the construction

**Conjecture.** Iterating the edge-partition/quotient construction using the finest
partition for which every quotient labeling is isometric converges, for finite connected
graphs, precisely to the class of partial cubes, and the fixed points among these under a
natural refinement order are exactly the median graphs.

**The key insight is** that isometry of the parity labeling is equivalent to the
partition refining the Djokovic–Winkler relation, whose transitivity is the defining
feature of partial cubes and whose median property singles out median graphs.

**Why now?** Median structures underpin phylogenetic networks and concept lattices;
a constructive parity-based test for "how close is this graph to a partial cube" would
give practitioners a quantitative defect measure rather than a yes/no classification.

## 4. Stretch spectra distinguish expanders from grids

**Conjecture.** The distribution of per-edge stretch values of the coordinate-hypercube
reading of the quotient labeling, taken over all singleton edge partitions, separates
bounded-degree expanders from bounded-genus graphs: expanders exhibit a heavy tail of
high-stretch edges while planar-like graphs concentrate near stretch one.

**The key insight is** that high stretch on an edge signals a short cycle carrying a large
class-parity weight, and the abundance of short independent cycles is exactly what
distinguishes expansion from planarity.

**Why now?** Cheap spectral-free proxies for expansion are valuable for network design and
for pre-conditioning; a purely combinatorial parity statistic that correlates with the
spectral gap would be attractive because it avoids eigenvalue computation entirely.

## 5. Group choice trades contraction against dimension

**Conjecture.** Replacing the elementary abelian 2-group by a general finite abelian group
in the quotient construction preserves the no-stretch property and strictly reduces the
achievable contraction, so that for every target contraction ratio there is an optimal
group whose exponent matches the length of the longest chordless cycle carrying nontrivial
class parity.

**The key insight is** that a generator of larger additive order can traverse a long cycle
in a single algebraic step, converting what would be many hypercube coordinates into one,
which is exactly the mechanism that turns contraction into dimension savings.

**Why now?** Modern hashing and sketching increasingly exploit structured non-binary
groups; understanding the contraction-versus-dimension trade-off would let a designer pick
the coarsest sketch that still respects a required distance guarantee.
